Lexicographic allocations and extreme core payoffs:  
the case of assignment games

Marina Núñezᵃ and Tamás Solymosiᵇ

October 15, 2014

**Abstract**

We consider various lexicographic allocation procedures for coalitional games with transferable utility where the payoffs are computed in an externally given order of the players. The common feature of the methods is that if the allocation is in the core, it is an extreme point of the core. We first investigate the general relationships between these allocations and obtain two hierarchies on the class of balanced games.

Secondly, we focus on assignment games and sharpen some of these general relationships. Our main result is the coincidence of the sets of lemarals (vectors of lexicographic maxima over the set of dual coalitionally rational payoff vectors), lemacols (vectors of lexicographic maxima over the core) and extreme core points. As byproducts, we show that, similarly to the core and the coalitionally rational payoff set, also the dual coalitionally rational payoff set of an assignment game is determined by the individual and mixed-pair coalitions, and present an efficient and elementary way to compute these basic dual coalitional values. This provides a way to compute the Alexia value (the average of all lemacols) with no need to obtain the whole coalitional function of the dual assignment game.

*Keywords:* assignment game, extremal core allocations, Alexia value

1 Introduction
Assignment games (Shapley and Shubik, 1972) are models of assignment (two-
sided matching) markets with transferable utilities where the aim of each player
on one side is to form a proﬁtable coalition with a player on the other side. Since
only such bilateral cooperations have worth, these games are completely deﬁned
by the matrix containing the cooperative worths of all possible pairings of players
from the two sides.
Shapley and Shubik (1972) showed that the core of an assignment game is
precisely the set of dual optimal solutions to the assignment optimization problem
on the underlying matrix of mixed-pair proﬁts. This result not only implies that all
assignment games have a non-empty core but also that the core can be determined
without explicitly generating the entire coalitional function of the game. Typically,
the core of the assignment game contains inﬁnitely many allocations which makes
necessary some core selection.
The Shapley value (Shapley, 1953) is a well-known single-valued solution for
coalitional games with transferable utility. This value is the average of the marginal
payoﬀvectors, where the marginal payoﬀvector associated with a given ordering
of the set of agents is deﬁned by paying to each agent his marginal contribution to
the set of predecessors in the ordering. In an assignment game, each extreme core
allocation is a marginal payoﬀvector (Hamers et al., 2002). However, the converse
is not true and this is why the Shapley value of an assignment game may not select
a core allocation.
Another single-valued solution for coalitional games (with a non-empty core) is
the AL-value (Tijs et al., 2011), that is deﬁned as the average of the lexicographical
maximum core allocations or lemacols1. Given an order of the agents, the corre-
sponding lemacol is recursively deﬁned by paying to each agent the maximum he
can obtain inside the core under the restriction that his predecessors in the order
have already been paid their restricted maxima. By its deﬁnition, the AL-value
always selects a core allocation. For convex games (Shapley, 1971), lemacols and
the marginal worth vectors coincide.
For arbitrary transferable utility (TU) games, we obtain that when a marginal
worth vector is in the core, it coincides with the corresponding lemiral (the vector
of lexicograhic minima over the set of coalitionally rational payoﬀvectors) and also
with the lemaral (the vector of lexicographic maxima over the set of dual coali-
tionally rational payoﬀs) associated to the reverse order of the players. Similarly,
if a lemiral / lemaral is in the core, it coincides with the corresponding lemicol
/ lemacol (the vector of the lexicograhically minimized / maximized payoﬀs over
the core). The roles of the allocations in these implications are not symmetric.

lexicographic minimization (respectively maximization) over the set of coalitionally rational
payoﬀvectors (respectively over the set of dual coalitionally rational payoﬀvectors), where

3 Some relationships for σ-lexicographic allocations

We have seen so far that the aforementioned σ-lexicographical allocations present several

similarities. In this section we analyze under which circumstances the different payoff vectors

deﬁned from a same order σ do coincide. Later on, new σ-lexicographic allocations are

introduced by considering the dual game.

Moreover, we are interested in classes of games where either all extreme core payoff

vectors belong to one of the deﬁned classes of σ-lexicographic allocations, or conversely, all

outcomes of a given σ-lexicographic procedure are extreme core allocations. To this end, we

introduce the following deﬁnition.

A balanced game (N,w) is called

–ONTO-marginal (or ONTO-lemacol, or ONTO-lemicol, or ONTO-lemiral) if all its

extreme core points are marginal payoff vectors (or lemacols, or lemicols, or lemirals,

# Fair Core Imputations for the Assignment Game: New Solution Concepts and Efficient Algorithms

## Author

## Abstract

The assignment game is a classical model for profit sharing and a cornerstone of cooperative game theory. While an imputation in its core guarantees fairness among coalitions, it provides no fairness guarantee at the level of individual agents: single agents or one sided coalitions have zero standalone value and may receive arbitrarily small payoffs. Motivated by the growing focus on individual level fairness, we ask: Can one select a core imputation that is also fair to individuals? We introduce three individual fairness driven solution concepts, each promoting equity in a different way. The leximin and leximax core imputations extend max min and min max fairness to uplift the least advantaged and constrain the most advantaged agents, respectively. The min spread core imputation minimizes the gap between the largest and smallest positive payoffs, promoting equitable profit distribution. For all three solution concepts, we develop combinatorial, strongly polynomial algorithms. The leximin and leximax algorithms are based on a novel adaptation of the primal dual paradigm, while the min spread algorithm combines partial executions of the first two. We expect our work to revive innovation on the potent primal dual paradigm as well as promote further work on the algorithmic study of fairness and stability.

Fair item allocation problem

Egalitarian item allocation, also called max-min item allocation is a fair item allocation problem, in which the fairness criterion follows the egalitarian rule. The goal is to maximize the minimum value of an agent. That is, among all possible allocations, the goal is to find an allocation in which the smallest value of an agent is as large as possible. In case there are two or more allocations with the same smallest value, then the goal is to select, from among these allocations, the one in which the second-smallest value is as large as possible, and so on (by the leximin order). Therefore, an egalitarian item allocation is sometimes called a leximin item allocation. 

The special case in which the value of each item j to each agent is either 0 or some constant v_j is called the santa claus problem: santa claus has a fixed set of gifts, and wants to allocate them among children such that the least-happy child is as happy as possible.

L46: # Equitable Core Imputations via
L47: a New Adaptation of The Primal-Dual Framework
L48: 
L49: Vijay V. Vazirani Note: Supported in part by NSF grant CCF-2230414. Affiliation: University of California, Irvine
L50: ###### Abstract
L51: 
L52: The classic paper of Shapley and Shubik [cite34†SS71 ] characterized the core of the assignment game. We observe that a sub-coalition consisting of one player (or a set of players from the same side of the bipartition) can make zero profit, and therefore its profit under a core imputation can be an arbitrary amount. Hence an arbitrary core imputation makes no fairness guarantee at the level of individual agents. Can this deficiency be addressed by picking a “good” core imputation?
L53: To arrive at an appropriate solution concept, we give specific criteria for picking a special core imputation, and we undertake a detailed comparison of four solution concepts. Leximin and leximax core imputations come out as clear winners; we define these to be equitable core imputations. These imputations achieve “fairness” in different ways: whereas leximin tries to make poor agents more rich, leximax tries to make rich agents less rich.
L54: We give combinatorial strongly polynomial algorithms for computing these imputations via a novel adaptation of the classical primal-dual paradigm. The “engine” driving them involves insights into core imputations obtained via complementarity. It will not be surprising if our work leads to new uses of this powerful technique. Furthermore, we expect more work on computing the leximin and leximax core imputations of other natural games, in addition to the recent follow-up work [cite35†GGSV24 ].
L55: ## 1 Introduction
L56: Equality and fair division are timeless values which have taken centerstage in economics all the way from the early days of social choice theory [cite36†Arr51 ] to the Internet age [cite37†Mou19 ]. Within cooperative game theory, the core is considered the gold standard solution concept for “fair” profit sharing. It distributes the total worth of a game among the agents in such a way that the profit received by a sub-coalition is at least as large as the profit which the sub-coalition can generate all by itself.
L57: Thus a core imputation is fair to each of exponentially many sub-coalitions – a stringent requirement indeed. Additionally, it ensures stability of the grand coalition, since no sub-coalition has an incentive to secede.
L58: We observe that in the assignment game, which forms a paradigmatic setting for studying the notion of core of a transferable utility (TU) market game^{1}^{1} 1 In large part due to the classic work of Shapley and Shubik [cite34†SS71 ]., a sub-coalition consisting of one player (or a set of players from the same side of the bipartition) can make zero profit, and therefore its profit under a core imputation can be an arbitrary amount.
L59: Hence an arbitrary core imputation makes no fairness guarantee at the level of individual agents. Can this deficiency be addressed by picking a “good” core imputation? We will address this question.
L60: The prominent work of Dutta and Ray [cite38†DR89 ] sought a middle-ground in the tension between sub-coalitions demanding profit which is commensurate with their inherent worth and the societal norm of ‘‘equality’’ as a desirable outcome. They showed that a convex game^{2}^{2} 2 The characteristic function of such a game is supermodular, see Definition cite39†3 . admits a unique core imputation which Lorenz dominates all other core imputations; they call it the egalitarian solution.
L61: From our standpoint, [cite38†DR89 ] has three shortcomings: it does not apply to several key natural games, including the assignment, MST and max-flow games, since they are not convex; it is not efficiently computable for any non-trivial, natural game; and the Lorenz order is a partial, and not a total, order.
L62: At a high level, our goal is analogous to that of Dutta and Ray; however, we wish to rectify their three shortcomings; in particular, we wish to address the assignment game, which occupies a special place in cooperative game theory. To arrive at an appropriate solution concept, we give the following criteria for picking a special core imputation:
L63: 
L64:   1. 1.
L65: It should attempt to equalize the profit shares of individual agents, subject to constraints imposed by the core. In particular, for the assignment game, it should be equitable to both sides of the bipartition, unlike currently known methods; see Section cite10†3.1 .
L66: 
L67:   2. 2.
L68: It should be computable in polynomial time via a combinatorial algorithm^{3}^{3} 3 i.e., the algorithm does not invoke an LP-solver.. As is well-known, such algorithms provide non-trivial insights into the structure of the problem and the solution.
L69: Icing on the cake: It should be computable in strongly polynomial time.
L70: In Section cite15†5 we use these criteria to undertake a detailed comparison of four solution concepts: leximin and leximax core imputations, the nucleolus, and the core imputation that maximizes Nash social welfare, see Section cite16†5.1 for formal definitions. Leximin and leximax core imputations emerge as clear winners and we define these to be equitable core imputations.
L71: We give strongly polynomial algorithms for computing these imputations via a novel adaptation of the classical primal-dual paradigm, see Section cite7†1.1 . It will not be surprising if our work leads to new uses of this powerful technique.
L72: A useful perspective is provided by the stable matching game of Gale and Shapley [cite40†GS62 ], which is a non-transferable utility (NTU) game. The core of this game is the set of all stable matchings — each ensures that no coalition formed by one agent from each side of the bipartition has an incentive to secede. It is well known that this set forms a finite distributive lattice and hence the Birkhoff Representation Theorem applies [cite41†Bir37 ].
L73: The top and bottom elements of this lattice maximally favor one side and disfavor the other side of the bipartition. Furthermore, the Deferred Acceptance Algorithm of Gale and Shapley [cite40†GS62 ] can find only these two extreme matchings.
L74: Since several applications of this game call for stable matchings which are more equitable to both sides, the question of finding such matchings efficiently has garnered much attention, leading to efficient algorithms as well as intractability results, see [cite42†ILG87 , cite43†TS98 , cite44†Che10 , cite45†CMS11 , cite46†EIV23 ]. These efficient algorithms crucially use Birkhoff’s Representation Theorem for finite distributive lattices [cite41†Bir37 ] and the notion of rotations [cite47†IL86 ].
L75: Interestingly enough, the assignment game shares some features with the stable matching game, even though the former is TU and the latter is NTU. Shapley and Shubik [cite34†SS71 ] characterized the core of the assignment game: they showed that the set of its core imputations is precisely the set of optimal solutions to the dual of the LP-relaxation of the maximum weight matching problem in the underlying bipartite graph, where the weight of this matching is the worth of the game, see Section cite10†3.1 .
L76: Observe that the worth of the assignment game is given by an optimal solution to the primal LP and its core imputations are given by optimal solutions to the dual LP. The fundamental fact connecting these two solutions is complementary slackness conditions; its implications are explored in Section cite11†4 . The design of our primal and dual update steps critically uses these insights.
L77: By [cite34†SS71 ], the entire polytope of optimal dual solutions forms the core of this game. If the latter is not a singleton, it is a dense set consisting of uncountably many elements. Furthermore, this set supports the operations of meet and join, i.e., it forms a (non-finite) lattice. The top and bottom elements of this lattice form two extreme imputations, each maximally favoring one side and disfavoring the other side of the bipartition.
L78: So far efficient algorithms were known for computing only these two extreme imputations^{4}^{4} 4 Their convex combination is also a core imputation; however, it is not clear what fairness properties it possesses., which in a sense are the least fair among core imputations, see Section cite10†3.1 .
L79: We note that although the lattice of core imputations of the assignment game is distributive, it is not finite and therefore Birkhoff’s Representation Theorem does not apply to it. Hence a fresh approach was required for answering our question of picking a “more fair” core imputation. As stated above, our quest for an answer led to defining leximin and leximax core imputations as equitable core imputations.
L80: We expect more work on computing such imputations for other natural games, in addition to the current follow-up work [cite35†GGSV24 ]. We also expect a deeper exploration of properties of these imputations.
L81: ### 1.1 How was the Primal-Dual Framework Adapted to our Problem?
L82: 
L83: The primal-dual method has three distinguishing features:
L84: 
L85:   1. 1.
L86: 
L87: It provides a malleable, high level framework whose details can be custom-designed to the specific problem at hand.
L88: 
L89:   2. 2.
L90: 
L91: It is able to find a globally acceptable (optimal or near-optimal) solution by making only local improvements.
L92: 
L93:   3. 3.
L94: 
L95: It yields efficient, combinatorial algorithms.
L96: This method had major successes, first in combinatorial optimization [cite48†LP86 , cite49†Sch86 ] and then in approximation algorithms [cite50†Vaz01 ]. These settings involved finding an integral optimal (or near-optimal) solution to the primal LP, in tandem with an optimal (or near-optimal) solution to the dual LP. Complementary slackness conditions — or an appropriate relaxation of these conditions — helped transform the global task into a sequence of local tasks.
L97: Following these successes, researchers successfully adapted it to solve certain non-linear convex programs as well [cite51†DPSV08 , cite52†JV08 , cite53†Vaz12 , cite54†DGM16 ]. Indeed, today it is appropriate to call this method the primal-dual paradigm.
L98: A common thread in all these works is that the algorithm starts off with an easily-computed, suboptimal dual solution which is modified iteratively. An iteration ends when modifications are blocked; at this point a suitable integral change is made to the current primal solution to enable further modifications. When all (relaxed) complementary slackness conditions are satisfied, the algorithm terminates.
L99: Despite its malleability, there seemed little reason to pick this method for our problem. By Lemma cite55†3 , the leximin core imputation is unique. The closest comparison will be with the maximum weight matching problem in a bipartite graph – both problems seek an optimal, rather than near-optimal, solution. As is well known, a maximum weight matching appears at a vertex of the bipartite matching polytope, i.e., the polytope defined by the constraints of the primal LP (cite56†1 ).
L100: Therefore, the solution lies at one of finitely — though possibly exponentially — many points and a lot is known about their combinatorial properties to help design the algorithm. In contrast, at present we do not know where in the polytope of optimal dual solutions does the leximin (and leximax) core imputation lie, see Section cite30†9 .
L101: Computing optimal solutions to our primal and dual LPs, namely a maximum weight matching and a core imputation, is straightforward. Indeed, this is the first step in our current algorithm. Then starts the main problem, of transforming the arbitrary core imputation into a leximin or leximax imputation. However, the starting primal and dual solutions already satisfy all complementary slackness conditions, so how will the global problem be broken into local steps?
L102: Our answer emerged after reducing the primal-dual method to its bare bone essentials: The method involves two processes which alternately make local improvements to two entities. Additionally, a suitable mechanism is devised which nudges these local improvements towards a global solution.
L103: Our primal-dual algorithm for leximin core imputation works as follows: The dual update steps leximin-improve the current dual solution by altering the profits of certain vertices; however, the optimality of the dual is never tampered with. This process gets blocked when an unmatched edge is just about to go under-tight, which would lead to an infeasible dual. At this point, the primal-update step takes necessary actions so dual improvement can resume.
L104: Importantly, the set of matched edges is kept unchanged throughout. Hence, complementary slackness conditions, which held at the start of the algorithm, in fact hold throughout. Clearly, a different mechanism needs to be devised that transforms local improvements into a global solution.
L105: The answer to this question is another novel feature of our approach: in our case, the mechanism is a clock that helps synchronize all events. Indeed, the progress made by the algorithm is a direct function of time as follows: Let the given instance be $G=(U,V,E)$ with weight function $w:E\rightarrow\mathcal{Q}_{+}$.
L106: For each time $t$, we can identify a vertex set $W_{t}\subseteq(U\cup V)$ such that in the induced subgraph $H_{t}$ of $G$, the profit shares form the unique leximin core imputation for $H_{t}$. The proof of this fact crucially depends on the correct resolution of some subtle algorithmic choices, see Sections cite24†7.1 and cite27†7.3.1 . The set $W_{t}$ grows with time and we prove that in polynomial time $W_{t}=(U\cup V)$, hence terminating in the required imputation.
L107: We note that some previous primal-dual algorithms had also used the notion of time but it in a different and much less prominent manner. In [cite57†JV01 ] duals grow with time and this aspect is used for enforcing relaxed complementary slackness constraints; however, it is the latter which transform the global problem to a local one. [cite52†JV08 ] also grow duals with time.
L108: Again, it is not used for transforming the global problem to a local one, but for ensuring that the cost sharing method derived satisfies the property of cross-monotonicity.
L109: The broad outline given above is far from sufficient for designing the entire algorithm. The latter requires a precise understanding of the way core imputations allocate the total profit to agents and teams; in particular, we need to answer the following questions:
L110: 
L111:   1. 1.
L112: 
L113: Do core imputations spread the profit more-or-less evenly or do they restrict profit to certain well-chosen agents? If the latter, what characterizes these “chosen” agents?
L114: 
L115:   2. 2.
L116: An edge $(i,j)$ in the underlying graph is called a team. By definition, under any core imputation, the sum of profits of $i$ and $j$ is at least the weight of this edge. For which teams is the sum strictly larger?
L117: 
L118:   3. 3.
L119: 
L120: How do core imputations behave in the presence of degeneracy? An assignment game is said to be non-degenerate if it admits a unique maximum weight matching.
L121: 
L122: Our answers, using complementary slackness conditions and strict complementarity, are provided in Section cite11†4 .
L123: ## 2 Related Works
L124: 
L125: The importance of “fair” profit-sharing has been recognized for the proper functioning of all aspects of society — from personal relationships to business collaborations. Moreover, this has been a consideration since ancient times, e.g., see the delightful and thought-provoking paper by Aumann and Maschler [cite58†AM85 ], which discusses problems from the 2000-year-old Babylonian Talmud on how to divide the estate of a dead man among his creditors.
L126: Below we state results giving LP-based core imputations for natural games; these are also candidates for the study of leximin and leximax core imputations. Deng et al.
L127: [cite59†DIN99 ] gave LP-based characterization of the cores of several combinatorial optimization games, including maximum flow in unit capacity networks both directed and undirected, maximum number of edge-disjoint $s$-$t$ paths, maximum number of vertex-disjoint $s$-$t$ paths, maximum number of disjoint arborescences rooted at a vertex $r$, and general graph matching game in which the weight of optimal fractional and integral matchings are equal (such a game has a non-empty core).
L128: In a different direction, Vande Vate [cite60†Vat89 ] and Rothblum [cite61†Rot92 ] gave linear programming formulations for stable matchings; the vertices of their underlying polytopes are integral and are stable matchings. More recently, Kiraly and Pap [cite62†KP08 ] showed that the linear system of Rothblum is in fact totally dual integral (TDI). Recently, [cite63†Vaz24 ] gave the first game for which total unimodularity does not hold and total dual integrality is needed for characterizing its core.
L129: Interestingly, this game, called the investment management game, is a game against nature rather than a cooperative game.
L130: We next describe results for the facility location game. First, Kolen [cite64†Kol83 ] showed that for the unconstrained facility location problem, each optimal solution to the dual of the classical LP-relaxation is a core imputation if and only if this relaxation has no integrality gap. L15: cite7†View PDF cite8†HTML (experimental) L16: > Abstract:The assignment game is a classical model for profit sharing and a cornerstone of cooperative game theory. While an imputation in its core guarantees fairness among coalitions, it provides no fairness guarantee at the level of individual agents: single agents or one sided coalitions have zero standalone value and may receive arbitrarily small payoffs. Motivated by the growing focus on individual level fairness, we ask: Can one select a core imputation that is also fair to individuals?
L17: > We introduce three individual fairness driven solution concepts, each promoting equity in a different way. The leximin and leximax core imputations extend max min and min max fairness to uplift the least advantaged and constrain the most advantaged agents, respectively. The min spread core imputation minimizes the gap between the largest and smallest positive payoffs, promoting equitable profit distribution.
L18: > For all three solution concepts, we develop combinatorial, strongly polynomial algorithms. The leximin and leximax algorithms are based on a novel adaptation of the primal dual paradigm, while the min spread algorithm combines partial executions of the first two. We expect our work to revive innovation on the potent primal dual paradigm as well as promote further work on the algorithmic study of fairness and stability.

L16@P1: Abstract
L17@P1: We consider various lexicographic allocation procedures for coalitional games
L18@P1: with transferable utility where the payoffs are computed in an externally given
L19@P1: order of the players. The common feature of the methods is that if the allocation
L20@P1: is in the core, it is an extreme point of the core. We first investigate the general
L21@P1: relationships between these allocations and obtain two hierarchies on the class of
L22@P1: balanced games.
L23@P1: Secondly, we focus on assignment games and sharpen some of these general
L24@P1: relationships. Our main result is the coincidence of the sets of lemarals (vectors
L25@P1: of lexicographic maxima over the set of dual coalitionally rational payoff vectors),
L26@P1: lemacols (vectors of lexicographic maxima over the core) and extreme core points.
L27@P1: As byproducts, we show that, similarly to the core and the coalitionally rational
L28@P1: payoff set, also the dual coalitionally rational payoff set of an assignment game is
L29@P1: determined by the individual and mixed-pair coalitions, and present an efficient
L30@P1: and elementary way to compute these basic dual coalitional values. This provides
L31@P1: a way to compute the Alexia value (the average of all lemacols) with no need to
L32@P1: obtain the whole coalitional function of the dual assignment game.
L33@P1: Keywords: assignment game, extremal core allocations, Alexia value

L47@P2: Assignment games (Shapley and Shubik, 1972) are models of assignment (two-sided
L48@P2: matching) markets with transferable utilities where the aim of each player on one side is

L55@P2: assignment game contains infinitely many allocations which makes necessary some core

L44: # Fair Core Imputations for the Assignment Game:
L45: New Solution Concepts and Efficient Algorithms
L46: 
L47: Vijay V. Vazirani Note: Supported in part by NSF grant CCF-2230414. Affiliation: University of California, Irvine
L48: ###### Abstract
L49: 
L50: The assignment game is a classical model for profit-sharing and a cornerstone of cooperative game theory. While an imputation in its core guarantees fairness among coalitions, it provides no fairness guarantee at the level of individual agents: single agents or one-sided coalitions have zero standalone value and may receive arbitrarily small payoffs. Motivated by the growing focus on individual-level fairness, we ask: Can one select a core imputation that is also fair to individuals?
L51: We introduce three individual-fairness-driven solution concepts, each promoting equity in a different way. The leximin and leximax core imputations extend max–min and min–max fairness to uplift the least advantaged and constrain the most advantaged agents, respectively. The min-spread core imputation minimizes the gap between the largest and smallest positive payoffs, promoting equitable profit distribution.
L52: For all three solution concepts, we develop combinatorial, strongly polynomial algorithms. The leximin and leximax algorithms are based on a novel adaptation of the primal–dual paradigm, while the min-spread algorithm combines partial executions of the first two. We expect our work to revive innovation on the potent primal-dual paradigm as well as promote further work on the algorithmic study of fairness and stability.
L53: ## 1 Introduction
L54: Fairness and equitable division have long been central themes in economics, from early social choice theory [cite32†2 ] to modern challenges in Internet resource allocation [cite33†37 ]. The study of fairness has come to a basic truth: no single definition can universally capture fairness, e.g., [cite34†40 ] lists 21 definitions! Within this vast literature, we are concerned with fairness at the level of coalitions and individual fairness.
L55: For the former, the core is the gold standard solution concept: it ensures that no coalition has an incentive to secede by guaranteeing each coalition at least as much profit as they can achieve on their own. Hence a core imputation guarantees stability by allocating a fair profit to each of exponentially many coalitions—a stringent requirement indeed.
L56: Recent work across game theory, networking and resource allocation has renewed attention on individual-level fairness as a fundamental consideration, e.g., the wide spread use of max-min and min-max fairness [cite35†41 , cite36†7 , cite37†39 , cite38†43 ], as well as their extensions to leximin and leximax allocations in modern applications such as fair rent division [cite39†18 ] and citizens’ assemblies [cite40†15 ].
L57: Our work bridges these two traditions in the context of the assignment game, which occupies a central place within cooperative game theory; the classic work of Shapley and Shubik [cite41†47 ] gave a complete characterization of its core, see Section cite10†3.1 . In this game, a coalition consisting of a single agent or a group from one side of the bipartition has zero standalone value.
L58: Consequently, under an arbitrary core imputation, individual agents are allowed to receive arbitrary profit shares, leading to inequity. To address this deficiency, we seek a core imputation that satisfies two key criteria:

L60: 
L61: The allocation of profit shares is individually fair.
L62: 
L63:   2. 2.
L64: 
L65: It is computable in polynomial—or preferably, strongly polynomial—time via a combinatorial algorithm^{1}^{1} 1 That is, the algorithm does not invoke an LP-solver, e.g., see [cite42†46 , cite43†33 ].
L66: We propose three solution concepts. All three deal with profit shares of essential agents, i.e., agents which are matched in every maximum weight matching, see Section cite11†4 ; these are the only agents which get positive profits in core imputations.
L67: 
L68:   1. 1.
L69: 
L70: the leximin core imputation, which extends max-min fairness by maximizing the smallest individual share and, subject to that, the next smallest, and so on;
L71: 
L72:   2. 2.
L73: the leximax core imputation, which symmetrically extends min-max fairness by minimizing the largest share, then the second largest, and so on;
L74: 
L75:   3. 3.

L77: the min-spread core imputation, which minimizes the difference between the largest and smallest profit shares of essential agents.
L78: It is easy to see that none of these solution concepts dominates the others, e.g., see the example given in Section cite15†5 . Our solution concepts seek to reconcile the tension between coalitions demanding profit which is commensurate with their inherent worth and the societal norm of “equality” as a desirable outcome.
L79: Each promotes individual fairness in a distinct way: leximin uplifts the least advantaged, leximax reins in the most advantaged and min-spread makes individual profit shares as equal as possible. In Section cite15†5 we show that whereas leximin and leximax core imputations are unique, min-spread is not. In Section cite16†5.1 we show that the prominent solution concept of nucleolus does not promote individual fairness in any of these three ways, even for an infinite family of games, Theorem cite44†6 .
L80: We design combinatorial, strongly polynomial algorithms, having a running time of $O(mn^{3})$, for all three proposed solution concepts. For the leximin and leximax core imputations, our algorithms are based on a novel adaptation of the classical primal-dual paradigm; see Section cite7†1.1 . The algorithm for the min-spread solution is arguably even more innovative.
L81: It is made possible by the combinatorial nature of the previous two algorithms and is obtained by carefully orchestrating their partial executions, see Section cite27†10 .
L82: The assignment and stable matching games share a key structural property: in both, the set of solutions forms a distributive lattice, with the top and bottom elements favoring opposite sides of the bipartition (see details in Section cite8†2 ). These extreme solutions are efficiently computable in both settings. However, while the stable matching lattice is finite—enabling the design of algorithms for finding more equitable outcomes—the lattice of core imputations in the assignment game is infinite.

L100: The method achieved major successes, first in combinatorial optimization [cite43†33 , cite42†46 ] and then in approximation algorithms [cite46†51 ]. These settings involved finding an integral optimal (or near-optimal) solution to the primal LP, together with an optimal (or near-optimal) solution to the dual LP. Complementary slackness conditions — or an appropriate relaxation of these conditions — helped transform the global task into a sequence of local tasks.

L102: Despite its versatility, it was not initially clear that this method would be suitable for our setting. In our case, computing an optimal solution to the primal and dual LPs — namely, a maximum-weight matching and an associated core imputation — is straightforward. L122: ## 2 Related Works
L123: Comparison with the stable matching game: A useful perspective is provided by the stable matching game of Gale and Shapley [cite52†19 ], which is a non-transferable utility (NTU) game. The core of this game is the set of all stable matchings — each ensures that no coalition formed by one agent from each side of the bipartition has an incentive to secede. It is well known that this set forms a finite distributive lattice.
L124: Its top and bottom elements maximally favor one side and disfavor the other side of the bipartition, and the Deferred Acceptance Algorithm [cite52†19 ] computes precisely these two extremes.
L125: However, in many applications, one desires stable matchings that are more equitable to both sides. This has motivated considerable research on finding such matchings efficiently, leading to efficient algorithms as well as intractability results, see [cite53†25 , cite54†50 , cite55†6 , cite56†5 , cite57†13 ]. These efficient algorithms crucially use Birkhoff’s Representation Theorem for finite distributive lattices [cite58†4 ] and the notion of rotations [cite59†26 ].
L126: Shapley and Shubik [cite41†47 ] showed that the set of its core imputations is the entire polytope of optimal solutions to the dual of the LP-relaxation of the maximum weight matching problem in the underlying bipartite graph. If this set is not a singleton, it is a dense set consisting of uncountably many elements. Furthermore, this set forms an infinite distributive lattice.
